vsm1.7:43.1:
The World-sphere Mountains’ line of summits plunges down into the sea
Just two and eighty thousand leagues, and towers up in like degree,
vsm1.7:43.2: Enringing one world-element all round in its entirety.
vsm1.7:43.3: And the size of the Jambu (Rose-apple) Tree is the same as that of
vsm1.7:43.4: the Citrapāṭaliya Tree of the Asura demons, the Simbali Tree of the Garuḷa demons,
vsm1.7:43.5: the Kadamba Tree in the western continent of Aparagoyana, the Kappa Tree in the northern continent of the Uttarakurus,
vsm1.7:43.6:
the Sirīsa Tree in the eastern continent of Pubbavideha, and the Pāricchattaka
Tree in the heaven of the Deities of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa).
vsm1.7:43.8:
The Pāṭali, Simbali, and Jambu, the deities’ Pāricchattaka,
The Kadamba, the Kappa Tree and the Sirīsa as the seventh.
vsm1.7:44.1: Herein, the moon’s disk is forty-nine leagues across
vsm1.7:44.2: and the sun’s disk is fifty leagues.
vsm1.7:44.3: The realm of Tāvatiṃsa (the Thirty-three Gods) is ten thousand leagues.
vsm1.7:44.4: Likewise the realm of the Asura demons, the great Avīci (unremitting) Hell, and Jambudīpa (India).
vsm1.7:44.8: And herein, each great continent is surrounded by five hundred small islands.
vsm1.7:44.9: And the whole of that constitutes a single world-sphere, a single world-element.
vsm1.7:44.10: Between this and the adjacent world-spheres are the Lokantarika (world-interspace) hells.
vsm1.7:44.11: So the world-spheres are infinite in number, the world-elements are infinite,
vsm1.7:44.12: and the Blessed One has experienced, known and penetrated them with the infinite knowledge of the Enlightened Ones.
vsm1.7:45.1: Therefore this world of location was known to him in all ways too.
vsm1.7:45.2: So he is “knower of worlds” because he has seen the world in all ways.
vsm1.7:46.1: In the absence of anyone more distinguished for special qualities than himself,
vsm1.7:46.2: there is no one to compare with him, thus he is incomparable.
vsm1.7:46.3: For in this way he surpasses the whole world in the special quality of virtue,
vsm1.7:46.4: and also in the special qualities of concentration, understanding, deliverance, and knowledge and vision of deliverance.
vsm1.7:46.5: In the special quality of virtue he is without equal, he is the equal only of those other Enlightened Ones without equal,
vsm1.7:46.6: he is without like, without double, without counterpart; …
vsm1.7:46.7: in the special quality of knowledge and vision of deliverance he is … without counterpart,
vsm1.7:46.8: according as it is said: “I do not see in the world with its deities, its Māras and its Brahmās,
vsm1.7:46.9: in this generation with its ascetics and brahmans, with its princes and men,
vsm1.7:46.10: anyone more perfect in virtue than myself” (S I 139), with the rest in detail,
vsm1.7:46.11: and likewise in the Aggappasāda Sutta (A II 34; It 87), and so on,
vsm1.7:46.12:
and in the stanzas beginning, “I have no teacher and my like does not exist in all
the world” (M I 171), all of which should be taken in detail.
vsm1.7:47.1: He guides (sāreti) men to be tamed (purisa-damme), thus he is leader of men to be tamed (purisadammasārathī);
vsm1.7:47.2: he tames, he disciplines, is what is meant.
vsm1.7:47.3:
Herein, animal males (purisā) and human males, and non-human males that are not tamed but fit to be tamed
(dametuṃ yuttā) are “men to be tamed” (purisadammā).
vsm1.7:47.4: For the animal males, namely, the royal nāga (serpent) Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara,
vsm1.7:47.5: Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, the royal nāga Āravāḷa, the elephant Dhanapālaka, and so on,
vsm1.7:47.6: were tamed by the Blessed One, freed from the poison of defilement and established in the refuges and the precepts of virtue;
vsm1.7:47.7:
and also the human males, namely, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhas’ (Jains’) son, the brahman
student Ambaṭṭha, Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and so on;
vsm1.7:47.8: and also the non-human males, namely, the spirits Āḷavaka, Sūciloma and Kharaloma, Sakka Ruler of Gods, etc.,
vsm1.7:47.9: were tamed and disciplined by various disciplinary means.
vsm1.7:47.10:
And the following sutta should be given in full here: “I discipline men to be tamed sometimes gently,
Kesi, and I discipline them sometimes roughly, and I discipline them sometimes gently and roughly” (A II 112).
vsm1.7:48.1:
Then the Blessed One moreover further tames those already tamed, doing so by announcing the first jhāna, etc.,
respectively to those whose virtue is purified, etc., and also the way to the higher path to stream enterers, and so on.
vsm1.7:48.2: Or alternatively, the words incomparable leader of men to be tamed can be taken together as one clause.
vsm1.7:48.3: For the Blessed One so guides men to be tamed
vsm1.7:48.4: that in a single session they may go in the eight directions by the eight liberations without hesitation.
vsm1.7:48.5: Thus he is called the incomparable leader of men to be tamed.
vsm1.7:48.6:
And the following sutta passage should be given in full here: “Guided by the elephant-tamer,
bhikkhus, the elephant to be tamed goes in one direction …” (M III 222).
vsm1.7:49.1:
He teaches (anusāsati) by means of the here and now, of the life to come, and of the ultimate goal,
according as befits the case, thus he is the Teacher (satthar).
vsm1.7:49.2:
And furthermore this meaning should be understood according to the Niddesa thus: “‘Teacher (satthar)’:
the Blessed One is a caravan leader (satthar) since he brings home caravans (sattha).
vsm1.7:49.3: Just as one who brings a caravan home gets caravans across a wilderness, gets them across a robber-infested wilderness,
vsm1.7:49.4: gets them across a wild-beast-infested wilderness, gets them across a foodless wilderness, gets them across a waterless wilderness,
vsm1.7:49.5: gets them right across, gets them quite across, gets them properly across, gets them to reach a land of safety,
vsm1.7:49.6:
so too the Blessed One is a caravan leader, one who brings home the caravans, he gets them
across a wilderness, gets them across the wilderness of birth” (Nidd I 446).
vsm1.7:50.1: Of gods and men: devamanussānaṃ = devānañ ca manussānañ ca (resolution of compound).
vsm1.7:50.2: This is said in order to denote those who are the best and also to denote those persons capable of progress.
vsm1.7:50.3: For the Blessed One as a teacher bestowed his teaching upon animals as well.
vsm1.7:50.4:
For when animals can, through listening to the Blessed One’s Dhamma, acquire
the benefit of a suitable rebirth as support for progress,
vsm1.7:50.5: and with the benefit of that same support they come, in their second or third rebirth, to partake of the path and its fruition.
vsm1.7:51.1: Maṇḍūka, the deity’s son, and others illustrate this.
vsm1.7:51.2: While the Blessed One was teaching the Dhamma to the inhabitants of the city of Campā on the banks of the Gaggarā Lake, it seems,
vsm1.7:51.3: a frog (maṇḍūka) apprehended a sign in the Blessed One’s voice.
vsm1.7:51.4: A cowherd who was standing leaning on a stick put his stick on the frog’s head and crushed it.
vsm1.7:51.5: He died and was straight away reborn in a gilded, divine palace, twelve leagues broad in the realm of the Thirty-three (Tāvatiṃsa).
vsm1.7:51.6: He found himself there, as if waking up from sleep, amidst a host of celestial nymphs,
vsm1.7:51.7: and he exclaimed, “So I have actually been reborn here. What deed did I do?”
vsm1.7:51.8: When he sought for the reason, he found it was none other than his apprehension of the sign in the Blessed One’s voice.
vsm1.7:51.9: He went with his divine palace at once to the Blessed One and paid homage at his feet.
vsm1.7:51.10: Though the Blessed One knew about it, he asked him:
vsm1.7:51.11:
“Who now pays homage at my feet,
Shining with glory of success,
Illuminating all around
With beauty so outstanding?”
vsm1.7:51.12:
“In my last life I was a frog,
The waters of a pond my home;
vsm1.7:51.13:
A cowherd’s crook ended my life
While listening to your Dhamma” (Vv 49).
vsm1.7:51.14: The Blessed One taught him the Dhamma.
vsm1.7:51.15: Eighty-four thousand creatures gained penetration to the Dhamma.
vsm1.7:51.16: As soon as the deity’s son became established in the fruition of stream-entry he smiled and then vanished.
vsm1.7:52.1:
He is enlightened (buddha) with the knowledge that belongs to the fruit of liberation,
since everything that can be known has been discovered (buddha) by him.
vsm1.7:52.2: Or alternatively, he discovered (bujjhi) the four truths by himself
vsm1.7:52.4: thus and for other such reasons he is enlightened (buddha).
vsm1.7:52.5:
And in order to explain this meaning the whole passage in the Niddesa beginning thus:
“He is the discoverer (bujjhitar) of the truths, thus he is enlightened (buddha).
vsm1.7:52.6: He is the awakened (bodhetar) of the generation, thus he is enlightened (buddha)” (Nidd I 457),
vsm1.7:52.7: or the same passage from the Paṭisambhidā (Paṭis I 174), should be quoted in detail.
vsm1.7:53.1:
Blessed (bhagavant) is a term signifying the respect and veneration accorded to him
as the highest of all beings and distinguished by his special qualities.
vsm1.7:53.3:
“Blessed” is the best of words,
“Blessed” is the finest word;
Deserving awe and veneration,
Blessed is the name therefore.
vsm1.7:54.1: Or alternatively, names are of four kinds:
vsm1.7:54.2: denoting a period of life, describing a particular mark, signifying a particular acquirement, and fortuitously arisen,
vsm1.7:54.3: which last in the current usage of the world is called “capricious.”
vsm1.7:54.4:
Herein, names denoting a period of life are those such as “yearling calf” (vaccha),
“steer to be trained” (damma), “yoke ox” (balivaddha), and the like.
vsm1.7:54.5:
Names describing a particular mark are those such as “staff-bearer” (daṇḍin), “umbrella-bearer” (chattin),
“topknot-wearer” (sikhin), “hand possessor” (karin—elephant), and the like.
vsm1.7:54.6:
Names signifying a particular acquirement are those such as “possessor of the threefold clear vision”
(tevijja), “possessor of the six direct-knowledges” (chaḷabhiñña), and the like.
vsm1.7:54.7: Such names are Sirivaḍḍhaka (“Augmenter of Lustre”), Dhanavaḍḍhaka (“Augmenter of Wealth”), etc.,
vsm1.7:54.8: are fortuitously arisen names; they have no reference to the word-meanings.
vsm1.7:55.1: This name, Blessed, is one signifying a particular acquirement;
vsm1.7:55.2: it is not made by Mahā-Māyā, or by King Suddhodana, or by the eighty thousand kinsmen,
vsm1.7:55.3: or by distinguished deities like Sakka, Santusita, and others.
vsm1.7:55.4: And this is said by the General of the Law:
vsm1.7:55.5: “‘Blessed’: this is not a name made by a mother …
vsm1.7:55.6:
This name ‘Buddha,’ which signifies final liberation, is a realistic description of Buddhas (Enlightened Ones), the Blessed Ones,
together with their obtainment of omniscient knowledge at the root of an Enlightenment Tree” (Paṭis I 174; Nidd I 143).
vsm1.7:56.1: Now, in order to explain also the special qualities signified by this name they cite the following stanza:
vsm1.7:56.2:
Bhagī bhajī bhāgī vibhattavā iti
Akāsi bhaggan ti garū ti bhāgyavā
Bahūhi ñāyehi subhāvitattano
Bhavantago so bhagavā ti vuccati.

The reverend one (garu) has blessings (bhagī), is a frequenter (bhajī), a partaker (bhāgī), a possessor of what
has been analyzed (vibhattavā); He has caused abolishing (bhagga), he is fortunate (bhāgyavā), He has fully developed himself
(subhāvitattano) in many ways; He has gone to the end of becoming (bhavantago); thus is called “Blessed” (bhagavā).
vsm1.7:56.3: The meaning of these words should be understood according to the method of explanation given in the Niddesa (Nidd I 142).
vsm1.7:57.1: But there is this other way:
vsm1.7:57.2:
Bhāgyavā bhaggavā yutto bhagehi ca vibhattavā.
Bhattavā vanta-gamano bhavesu: bhagavā tato.

He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), possessed of abolishment (bhaggavā), associated with blessings
(yutto bhagehi), and a possessor of what has been analyzed (vibhattavā).

He has frequented (bhattavā), and he has rejected going in the kinds of becoming
(VAnta-GAmano BHAvesu), thus he is Blessed (Bhagavā).
vsm1.7:58.1:
Herein, by using the characteristic of language beginning with “vowel augmentation of syllable,
elision of syllable” (see Kāśikā VI.3.109),
vsm1.7:58.2: or by using the characteristic of insertion beginning with the example of pisodara, etc. (see Pāṇini, Gaṇapāṭha 6, 3, 109),
vsm1.7:58.3:
it may be known that he can also be called “blessed” (bhagavā) when he can be called “fortunate” (bhāgyavā)
owing to the fortunateness (bhāgya) to have reached the further shore of the ocean of perfection of giving,
virtue, etc., which produce mundane and supramundane bliss (See Khp-a 108.).
vsm1.7:59.2:
as the three roots of the unprofitable, kinds of misconduct, defilement, stains, fictitious perceptions,
applied thoughts, and diversifications; as the four perversenesses,
vsm1.7:59.3:
cankers, ties, floods, bonds, bad ways, cravings, and clingings; as the five wildernesses in the heart,
shackles in the heart, hindrances, and kinds of delight;
vsm1.7:59.4:
as the six roots of discord, and groups of craving; as the seven inherent tendencies; as the eight wrongnesses;
as the nine things rooted in craving; as the ten courses of unprofitable action; as the sixty-two kinds of false view;
vsm1.7:59.5: as the hundred and eight ways of behaviour of craving—
vsm1.7:59.6:
or in brief, the five Māras, that is to say, the Māras of defilement, of the aggregates,
and of kamma-formations, Māra as a deity, and Māra as death.
vsm1.7:59.7: And in this context it is said:
vsm1.7:59.8:
He has abolished (bhagga) greed and hate,
Delusion too, he is canker-free;
vsm1.7:59.9:
Abolished every evil state,
“Blessed” his name may rightly be.
vsm1.7:60.1:
And by his fortunateness (bhāgyavatā) is indicated the excellence of his material
body which bears a hundred characteristics of merit;
vsm1.7:60.2: and by his having abolished defects (bhaggadosatā) is indicated the excellence of his Dhamma body.
vsm1.7:60.3:
Likewise, by his fortunateness is indicated the esteem of worldly people; and by his having
abolished defects, the esteem of those who resemble him.
vsm1.7:60.4:
And by his fortunateness it is indicated that he is fit to be relied on by laymen; and by his having
abolished defects that he is fit to be relied on by those gone forth into homelessness;
vsm1.7:60.5: and when both have relied on him, they acquire relief from bodily and mental pain
vsm1.7:60.6: as well as help with both material and Dhamma gifts,
vsm1.7:60.7: and they are rendered capable of finding both mundane and supramundane bliss.
vsm1.7:61.1:
He is also called “blessed” (bhagavā) since he is “associated with blessings”
(bhagehi yuttattā) such as those of the following kind,
vsm1.7:61.2: in the sense that he “has those blessings” (bhagā assa santi).
vsm1.7:61.3: Now, in the world the word “blessing” is used for six things, namely, lordship, Dhamma, fame, glory, wish, and endeavour.
vsm1.7:61.4: He has supreme lordship over his own mind,
vsm1.7:61.5: either of the kind reckoned as mundane and consisting in “minuteness, lightness,” etc., or that complete in all aspects,
vsm1.7:61.7: And he has exceedingly pure fame, spread through the three worlds, acquired though the special quality of veracity.
vsm1.7:61.8:
And he has glory of all limbs, perfect in every aspect, which is capable of comforting
the eyes of people eager to see his material body.
vsm1.7:61.9:
And he has his wish, in other words, the production of what is wanted, since whatever is wanted and needed by him
as beneficial to himself or others is then and there produced for him.
vsm1.7:61.10: And he has the endeavour, in other words, the right effort, which is the reason why the whole world venerates him.
vsm1.7:62.1:
He can also be called “blessed” (bhagavā) when he can be called “a possessor of what has been analyzed” (vibhattavā)
owing to his having analyzed and clarified all states into the three classes beginning with the profitable;
vsm1.7:62.2: or profitable, etc., states into such classes as aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, etc.;
vsm1.7:62.3: or the noble truth of suffering into the senses of oppressing, being formed, burning, and changing;
vsm1.7:62.4: and that of origin into the senses of accumulating, source, bond, and impediment;
vsm1.7:62.5: and that of cessation into the senses of escape, seclusion, being unformed, and deathless;
vsm1.7:62.6: and that of the path into the senses of outlet, cause, seeing, and predominance.
vsm1.7:62.7: Having analyzed, having revealed, having shown them, is what is meant.
vsm1.7:63.1: And because he has frequented the heavenly, divine, and noble abidings,
vsm1.7:63.3: and the void, desireless, and signless liberations,
vsm1.7:63.4:
and has cultivated and repeatedly practiced other mundane and supramundane higher-than-human states, he is called
“Blessed” (bhagavā) where “one who has frequented” (bhattavā) would be said.
vsm1.7:64.1:
He can also be called “blessed” (bhagavā) when he can be called one who “has rejected
going in the kinds of becoming” (vantagamano bhavesu) because in the three kinds of becoming (bhava),
the going (gamana), in other words, craving, has been rejected (vanta) by him.
vsm1.7:64.2:
And the syllables bha from the word bhava, and ga from the word gamana, and va from the word
vanta with the letter a lengthened, make the word bhagavā,
vsm1.7:64.3:
just as is done in the world of the grammarians outside the Dispensation with the word mekhalā
(waist-girdle) since “garland for the private parts” (MEhanassa KHAssa māLĀ) can be said.
vsm1.7:65.1:
As long as the meditator recollects the special qualities of the Buddha in this way, “For this and this
reason the Blessed One is accomplished, … for this and this reason he is blessed,”
vsm1.7:65.2: then: “On that occasion his mind is not obsessed by greed,
vsm1.7:65.3: or obsessed by hate, or obsessed by delusion;
vsm1.7:65.4: his mind has rectitude on that occasion, being inspired by the Perfect One” (A III 285).
vsm1.7:66.1: So when he has thus suppressed the hindrances by preventing obsession by greed, etc.,
vsm1.7:66.2: and his mind faces the meditation subject with rectitude,
vsm1.7:66.3: then his applied thought and sustained thought occur with a tendency toward the Enlightened One’s special qualities.
vsm1.7:66.4:
As he continues to exercise applied thought and sustained thought upon the Enlightened
One’s special qualities, happiness arises in him.
vsm1.7:66.5: With his mind happy, with happiness as a proximate cause, his bodily and mental disturbances are tranquilized by tranquillity.
vsm1.7:66.6: When the disturbances have been tranquilized, bodily and mental bliss arise in him.
vsm1.7:66.7: When he is blissful, his mind, with the Enlightened One’s special qualities for its object, becomes concentrated,
vsm1.7:66.8: and so the jhāna factors eventually arise in a single moment.
vsm1.7:66.9:
But owing to the profundity of the Enlightened One’s special qualities, or else
owing to his being occupied in recollecting special qualities of many sorts,
vsm1.7:66.10: the jhāna is only access and does not reach absorption.
vsm1.7:66.11:
And that access jhāna itself is known as “recollection of the Buddha” too, because it
arises with the recollection of the Enlightened One’s special qualities as the means.
vsm1.7:67.1: When a bhikkhu is devoted to this recollection of the Buddha, he is respectful and deferential towards the Master.
vsm1.7:67.2: He attains fullness of faith, mindfulness, understanding and merit.
vsm1.7:67.3: He has much happiness and gladness.
vsm1.7:67.5: He is able to endure pain.
vsm1.7:67.6: He comes to feel as if he were living in the Master’s presence.
vsm1.7:67.7: And his body, when the recollection of the Buddha’s special qualities dwells in it,
vsm1.7:67.8: becomes as worthy of veneration as a shrine room.
vsm1.7:67.9: His mind tends toward the plane of the Buddhas.
vsm1.7:67.10: When he encounters an opportunity for transgression,
vsm1.7:67.11: he has awareness of conscience and shame as vivid as though he were face to face with the Master.
vsm1.7:67.12: And if he penetrates no higher, he is at least headed for a happy destiny.
vsm1.7:67.13:
Now, when a man is truly wise,
His constant task will surely be
vsm1.7:67.14:
This recollection of the Buddha
Blessed with such mighty potency.
vsm1.7:67.15: This, firstly, is the section dealing with the recollection of the Enlightened One in the detailed explanation.
